p2.key:
Only the most energetic molecules have enough energy to overcome the intermolecular forces and escape from the surface.

The molecules left behind therefore have a lower average kinetic energy, so the temperature of the liquid falls.

The vapour pressure is the same in all three containers.

Once liquid and vapour are in dynamic equilibrium (rate of evaporation = rate of condensation), the vapour pressure depends only on temperature (and the liquid), not on the amount of liquid or the volume of the container, provided some liquid remains.

p2.key: At the melting point there is a dynamic equilibrium H2O(s) ⇌ H2O(l): molecules leave the ice to join the water and water molecules join the ice [1], at the same rate [1], so the amounts of ice and water stay constant.
Molecules at the surface with enough energy overcome intermolecular forces and evaporate [1]. Evaporation is endothermic: the energy is taken from the skin, which feels cool [1].
Ammonia molecules are in rapid, random, constant motion, so they diffuse (spread out) through the air and reach your nose.

Less time is needed: at higher temperature the molecules have greater average kinetic energy / move faster, so diffusion is faster.

Do not accept just "more energy" – the answer must refer to faster movement.
The average kinetic energies are the same, because the average KE of gas particles is proportional to the absolute (Kelvin) temperature, and both gases are at the same temperature.
Methane molecules have the greater average velocity. KE = ½mv2 is the same for both, and CH4 (Mr 16) is lighter than O2 (Mr 32), so v must be larger. Comments about molecule size score no mark.
Draw a smooth curve rising increasingly steeply (not a straight line) as temperature increases. It crosses 101.3 kPa at the boiling point, 100 °C.

p2.key: With lower atmospheric pressure, the vapour pressure of water equals the atmospheric pressure at a lower temperature, so water boils below 100 °C. Just saying the boiling point is reduced does not score.

p2.key:
Any three:

  • In a closed system, at equilibrium the rate at which molecules escape from the liquid equals the rate at which they return to it.
  • At a higher temperature, molecules have greater average kinetic energy.
  • So a greater proportion of molecules have enough energy to escape from the surface.
  • The vapour concentration (pressure) must rise until the return rate again equals the faster escape rate, so vapour pressure increases.
Read the temperature where the vapour pressure curve reaches 60.0 kPa: about 87 °C (86–88 °C).
